THE ANALYST’S SENSITIVITY TO EMOTIONAL NUANCE

To be sensitive to the subjective experience of others and of ourselves requires our increased sensitivity to the range of feeling states. We tend to be simplistic and think only of the major, or what may be called the massive, states of feeling, such as depression, despair, resentment, anger, rage. Most of these the patient can tell us about, can verbalize. But at times a far wider range of feeling states is present than we psychoanalysts and psychologists are prone to consider. Our compass of emotion tends to include love, hate, resentment, ambivalence, anger/rage, depression/despair/grief, elation/mania, anxiety, shame, and guilt. This list omits many more terms, often with nuances that we are tempted to homogenize away, thus closing off our awareness of the related experience. Some closing off of exploration unfortunately lies at our door. We need the poet’s range!

 —Rose Spiegel*

ROSE SPIEGEL’S STATEMENT issues a challenge to us as analysts. We must become attuned to the subtle shadings of emotional experiences in ourselves and our patients. Awareness of major shifts is insufficient. Like the poet who can capture fine gradations of meaning in apt phrases, we must be able to catch hold of minute degrees of our own and others’ emotions just as they make their appearance, so that we may search for adequate words to embody them. We sense the subtle appearance of a feeling in ourselves or our patients, and we must apprehend—later, perhaps, comprehend—its quality. Well-chosen words may help us move from apprehension to comprehension, but the whole process depends on that initial noticing of a subtle emotional experience.

FROM CHILDHOOD TO ADULTHOOD AND BACK AGAIN*

WHEN I WAS A CHILD, my mother periodically talked about her father dying in a Nazi concentration camp. I remember vividly how tears would well up in her eyes whenever she spoke about her father. On those occasions, I felt a tremendous compassion for my mother and an inarticulate helplessness to make her feel better or bring her father back to her. During my growing-up years, the Nazis and their death-dealing camps came to personify the ultimate, incomprehensible evil.

As an adult I have been intensely curious about the psychology of the Nazi-Jewish relationship. What are the underlying meanings and fantasies of Nazi ideology? How do Jews and what they represent fit into that ideology?

One could say that I have sublimated my fury about those who hurt my mother and killed my grandfather into an inquiry about the whys and wherefores of Nazi genocide. When we disagree with someone, we often attempt intellectually to destroy the integrity of his hated or unacceptable behavior by analyzing it into its constituent parts—its hidden motives and reasons. The psychoanalytic quest for knowledge in the subterranean depths of the unconscious is based largely on this sort of “civilizing” of aggression. Although I can be infuriated at the Nazis, I also must find a way to balance my indignation with my ethic of psychological mindedness, and not put the pursuit of understanding on hold.

I believe, however, that for many people who eschew understanding in favor of condemnation, there is a fear that knowing why someone does something is tantamount to excusing or condoning that person’s actions. Transcending The Self

The abandonment of classical psychoanalytic theory by many contemporary analysts and the proliferation of psychoanalytic theories proposed to replace it has inevitably resulted in the question of what specific changes in clinical strategy result from differing theoretical orientations. Object-relations theories are among the most widely discussed alternatives to classical psychoanalytic theory, and many analysts purport to apply them in psychoanalytic practice. Nonetheless, it remains unclear what specific changes in clinical technique result from an object-relations theoretical orientation. One of the difficulties in linking specific clinical interventions to object-relations theories emanates from the fact that these theories differ considerably and, at times, conflict with each other. Despite these differences, there is a commonality of underlying principles in the work of theorists such as Winnicott, Kohut, Fairbairn, and Guntrip, who emphasize the self and the role of the object in its development, that suggests an object-relations paradigm for psychoanalysis. The purpose here is to use this paradigm to delineate an integrated object-relations concept of therapeutic action and demonstrate how this model informs and ultimately shapes the psychoanalytic process.

A Review of A Prophetic Analyst: Erich Fromm’s Contributions to Psychoanalysis, edited by Mauricio Cortina, M.D., and Michael Maccoby, Ph.D. Northvale, NJ: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1996. 461 pp.

Earl Witenberg M.D.

Earl Witenberg

Earl G. Witenberg, M.D.
20 West 74th Street
New York, NY 10023

Earl Witenberg  

ERICH FROMM WAS A “RESPECTED WRITER” whose ideas influenced intellectual debate in the 1940s and 1950s. He was in those decades the most popular author to bring sociological analysis into integration with depth psychology. He lost some influence by crossing academic disciplines; he was no respecter of the rigidity of departmental boundaries. Herbert Marcuse also hurt Fromm’s reputation among the political left. He characterized Fromm as a neo-Freudian with a superficial culturalist outlook who distorted Freud by describing him as a radical philosopher.

For people at the White Institute, which Fromm cofounded, it is interesting to note that Fromm emigrated to Mexico in 1950 because of his wife’s illness; while there he began the Mexican Psychoanalytic Institute. He had been chairman of the faculty and of the Training Committee at White from 1946 to 1950. After his move, he visited New York for three months each year, at which time he was available for consultation by Institute members. He also continued to give seminars annually.

During those years he would expound on how he viewed Freud’s instinctual approach to be metaphoric rather than literal. He noted his close affinity with Freud’s intellectual legacy. However, he reformulated Freud’s belief that the infant’s primary drive was to minimize tension and seek pleasure, insisting instead that the infant’s (and the adult’s) primary need is to establish affectional ties that provide a sense of security and belonging.

Early on, Fromm discovered he could bypass the mainstream psychoanalytic community and did not need its approval. His free-ranging contributions intersperse a radical critique of society with a commitment to and analysis of humanistic values and ideals.

His contributions remain relevant, as evidenced by the papers gathered together in A Prophetic Analyst. Almost all of the papers were presented at the Erich Fromm International Symposium, May 1994.

Fromm never wrote a clinical psychoanalytic study.

Rebecca Curtis Ph.D.

Rebecca Curtis

Rebecca Curtis, Ph.D.
Derner Institute, Adelphi University
Garden City, NY 11530.

Rebecca Curtis  

SEXUALITY, TRAUMA, AND CREATIVITY—how are they related? Seeing chapter titles on these topics, many readers will be attracted to Joyce McDougall’s latest book. It is an extension of McDougall’s fascinating case studies and her ideas about “neosexualities” introduced in

153

her previous work. Woven into the narrative are McDougall’s own reactions to patients, including her dreams, written in a fascinating and readable style.

McDougall’s major thesis is that eroticization is a means of coping with early trauma. When such a defense fails, the archaic sexual impulses are foreclosed from consciousness, resulting in somaticization. She presents a number of cases, many of which she has discussed previously, to support this argument. I think she is convincing.

Known for her interesting and original insights about mind-body connections, McDougall is at her best when discussing this topic. She describes a primitive body language, a protolanguage, intended to communicate to the other world in the early life of the individual. The task of analysis, as she sees it, is to translate “bio-logic into psycho-logic.” Her thinking and rich case examples show a convergence with recent research that demonstrates the subsequent illnesses of people who say they are unaware of experiencing any emotional distress while they show physiological indications of such distress (Pennebaker, 1990).

In McDougall’s view, the deviant, or “neosexual,” have circumvented castration anxiety and Klein’s depressive position. She seems to include homosexuals in this group. Many interpersonal and relational analysts will have difficulty with her Freudian assumptions about the centrality of castration anxiety. These are recast from her previous (1980) ideas about concerns of the fate of the woman’s penis into the view, in this volume, that the girl fears her insides will be annihilated. McDougall’s idea is that men and women who develop neosexualities are trying to play out the illusion that castration is harmless and, indeed, exciting without danger. The primal scene and its significance are disavowed. For these people, the reality of castration anxiety, the difference and limitations of having only a male or female reproductive capability, and the disappointment at not being the sole object of desire of the parents is never acknowledged.

THE ISSUE ADDRESSED in this well-written, intentionally provocative, and strongly opinionated book is one that psychoanalysts have been wrestling with for years: whether or not it is ever, under any circumstances, justifiable to breach the confidentiality of the patientanalyst relationship. Because the last few years have seen the increasing spread of mandated child-abuse reporting laws, the application of the duty-to-warn obligation contained in the Tarasoff decision, and most pertinently, the spread of managed care and its reporting requirements, the issue has newly urgent salience.

For this book, Christopher Bollas, a prominent, prolific, British-trained-and-based psychoanalyst, has joined David Sundelson, a California lawyer schooled in literature and psychoanalysis. Their central premise is that any intrusion into the essential confidentiality of the analytic relationship does it irreparable harm. The patient’s fundamental process of conveying everything that comes to mind is irrevocably compromised if the patient knows that somehow, someday, something revealed may have to be communicated to others, perhaps to the patient’s detriment.

185 East 85th Street

Arthur Feiner  

WHEN I LEARNED THAT ROSE was seriously ill I thought, “No . . . this can’t be” I think that that denial would have been typical of each one of us, on hearing the news. Not Rose! But it was true; I quickly realized this when I went to Lenox Hill Hospital to see her.

She lay there quietly, not appearing to be in pain or distress. Her forehead was warm; but her hands were limp and icy. Her eyes didn’t blink—but she didn’t seem to be staring into space. She said nothing. Then she turned her head and seemed to look at my cane. I thought, “It’s the Rose I know, wondering what’s wrong with me.” I said, “Rose, you have to get well and go back to work. I have this cane because I hurt my instep and I’m getting better.”

I stood quietly for a few minutes. Then the nurse signalled me out, and as I left, I had all kinds of ambivalent thoughts: “She’ll make it . . . she won’t.” A few hours later her secretary called to tell me that Rose had died peacefully.

So a light, a beacon—one that we assumed would shine brightly forever, one that stood in our minds for “always”—went out.

We never thought it would happen to this incredible woman. She was our colleague, our model, our teacher, our supervisor, our committee member, our questioner, challenger, sometimes medical advisor, our friend for so many years. To some of us, she had been all these things since 1947, when she became the first graduate of our institute, and had begun her remarkable career in psychoanalysis, especially at White.

Her passing is a double blow and shock to us. Her brilliance had its own unique glow, and, at the same time, typified the continuous, growing, searching vitality of our psychoanalytic community. It was her gift to us, one out of her generous basket of many. And those gifts were always available, without the implicit obligation placed on the recipient.

Eulogy For Rose Spiegel, M.D.

Gerard Chrzanowski M.D.

Gerard Chrzanowski

Gerard Chrzanowski  

MY ACQUAINTANCE WITH ROSE goes back to the early days of the Institute, when classes were still held at the Croydon, a hotel on West 86th Street, and to my earliest days as a candidate at the Institute. Rose was actually the first person that I met after having been accepted as a candidate. It was never clear to me whether Rose had appointed herself as a welcoming committee, or whether that had been her assignment. Needless to say, her interest in acquainting me with the “rules and regulations” was a welcome antidote to whatever misgivings I may have had at that time about starting analytic training. Rose introduced me to the important people at the Institute. And although she talked freely and with pride about her medical career—she had graduated medical school with honors—she did not mention anything about her earlier life and background. It was as if for her, life had started once she had become acquainted with psychoanalysis. Clearly her main interest had become psychoanalysis and her excitement about matters psychoanalytic was palpable and contagious. In a way, she adopted the role of a big sister with me; we sat together at meetings in which she was always an active and lively participant.

After I graduated from training I lost contact with Rose until a good twenty years later. We both were busy, and it took until 1962 for our interests to begin to converge. That was the year of the first meeting of the International Federation of Psychoanalytic Societies, an organization that was being founded jointly by the White Institute, Fromm’s Mexican institute, the reconstituted German analytic group, and a Vienna-based institute. Rose attended the first meeting and her indomitable curiosity soon extended to questioning the role of analysis in former Nazi Germany. How did analysts who did not have to leave Germany, but had to disavow Freud, manage to conduct analyses, when they were always under the potential scrutiny of an informer? Were such analyses indeed possible?

IN ADAM PHILLIP’S MOST RECENT collection of essays, Terrors and Experts, he once again wields his formidable literary gifts to fashion a psychoanalytic sensibility well worth pondering. This sensibility is less interested in whether psychoanalysis is true than in what it can do for us. And what psychoanalysis can do for us, according to Phillips, is to make life a great deal more interesting and worth living. It is, in his words, an “interesting hedonism.”

Phillips’s point of departure is his reading of Freud as a master of irony. Open the toolkit of psychoanalysis and one finds juxtaposed two distinct “Freuds.” First, there is the well-known “Enlightenment Freud.” The Enlightenment Freud “ascribes needs—which he calls instincts—to people and then shows us how and why we try to disown them” (p. 6). He defines a set of essential terrors which, he assumes, we cannot bear to remember or know. He catalogues a variety of psychic mechanisms by which we remain unaware. He cures us by disabusing us of our self-motivated ignorance. Enlightenment Freud, in other words, fashions a grand new science of self-knowing.

But side-by-side with this Enlightenment Freud is a post-Freudian version of himself. This “post-Freudian Freud” dismantles his own Enlightenment project of efficient knowledge. He is an expert on the limits of expertise and the impossibility of self-knowledge. He is the master of suspicion, wondering what we can ever really know about the self, or whether there is ever really a self to know.

JEREMY HAZELL HAS WRITTEN what will likely be the definitive study of the life and work of Harry Guntrip. The heart of this compelling book is the distillation of Guntrip’s voluminous journals, including dreams and dream analyses recorded over a forty-year period, plus detailed postmeeting recordings of hundreds of analytic sessions with W. R. D. Fairbairn and D. W. Winnicott. In reporting these transactions, Guntrip focuses on, and Hazell emphasizes, the efforts to wrest new meanings from what transpires in the analytic encounters.

No other psychoanalyst has so exposed his suffering and struggles as has Harry Guntrip in his driving quest for self-knowledge and healing, and his secondary aim to extend clinically relevant psychoanalytic theory.

Organizing this copious material into an engrossing psychological odyssey was a labor of love. Hazell, a psychoanalytic psychotherapist in Cardiff, Wales, had had a five-year training analysis with Guntrip and later became an intimate friend. In 1994, Hazell published Personal Relations Therapy: The Collected Papers of H. J. S. Guntrip, a book that brought together Guntrip’s many contributions to psychoanalytic theory and practice.

Guntrip is best known for his clinical studies of schizoid individuals and for his extensions to Fairbairn’s theory of the endopsychic world. In 1968, when I read Guntrip’s book Schizoid Phenomena, Object Relations and the Self, it was his lucid phenomenology of the schizoid experience and his differentiation of the schizoid state from the dynamics of depression that most captured my interest and influenced my clinical approach.

As an example of passages I marked then, Guntrip wrote about the schizoid individual’s resistance to analysis. He said it was due, in part, to “the fear of humiliation over disclosing weakness, and deepest of all the sheer fear of collapse into a self which is too weak and fear-ridden to face living.

Peter Schneider

Peter Schneider  

DESPITE FREUD’S FAMOUS STATEMENT of his lack of affinity for the “oceanic feeling,” meditation and altered states of consciousness have long been of interest to psychotherapists of many different persuasions, including psychoanalysts and nonclinical psychologists. Jung had more than a passing interest in Buddhist and Taoist thought and meditative states of consciousness. Two prominent interpersonalists, Fromm and Horney, became interested in Zen in the later stages of their careers. There was an efflorescence of interest in various schools of meditation in the early to mid seventies among researchers of consciousness, such as Tart (1972, 1975) and Naranjo and Ornstein (1971). Psychodynamic psychiatrist and researcher Arthur Deikman published a work linking therapy and meditation (1982). Since the mid eighties, there has been a small but steady stream of work that attempts to integrate various kinds of meditation, ranging from transcendental meditation to zazen, with various Western psychological perspectives. Two collections typifying this effort are a British anthology edited by West (1987) and an American one edited by Katz (1983). The two works reviewed here are part of that continuing stream, as well as products of a current resurgence of interest in Buddhist meditation among psychologists, therapists, and a small but growing lay public. The works draw on the Tibetan Buddhist tradition, the vipassana or mindfulness meditation tradition (a Southeast Asian school akin to Zen), and, of course, Western psychology.

Thoughts Without a Thinker has been acclaimed by respected writers from both of the traditions from which it arose, psychoanalytic therapy and Tibetan Buddhist meditation.

Summary

Both of the patients mentioned above exemplify the turmoil of primitive anxiety and identity loss contaminated by a persecutory satanic presence. Like the clinical work with these two patients, a fictional analysis of the therapeutic process with Count Dracula would have shaped an interactional struggle to locate satanic aspects of the self and to remain free from fragmentation. The followers of Sullivan as well as the British object-relations theorists have stressed the effects of components of primitive anxiety during the analytic exchange. In Klein’s thinking, psychotic states contain elements of greed and the fantasized destruction of the envied breast, whereas Fairbairn finds oral conflicts and the fear of fusion in even the most regressed schizophrenic’s fantasies. For Sullivan and more contemporary interpersonalists, the primitive anxiety of psychotic states stems from unimaginable dissociated anxieties, while even the most bizarre symptoms serve defensive purposes for the seriously disturbed patient who is invited to join a collaborative inquiry about the dynamics of his or her illness.

Current psychoanalytic theories about severely impaired relatedness have surpassed either simple deficit or conflict models in favor of internalized relational configurations in core psychotic states. With the emergence of overtly psychotic states during analytic work, referential processes about satanic intrusion reflect impending identity loss and enactments of dissociated aspects of primitive anxiety. From an interpersonal perspective, re-created threats of annihilation and identity loss involve mutative, dyadic interactions that exceed either projection or the containment of projections. The analyst’s potential impact on the psychotic or borderline patient’s threatened self-cohesion, therefore, merits as much scrutiny as does the patient’s involving the analyst in the anxieties of nonhuman or demonic relatedness.

FROM MYTH TO PSYCHOANALYSIS*

BY WHATEVER NAME, emotional illness as a vicissitude of human existence has been with us for as long as we know anything of humankind. As long as there has been death and miscarriages of mourning, unrequited love, failure of ambition and the fading of faculties, vulnerability to sorrow, despair, and depression, there has been emotional illness. We know of no Golden Age of immunity.

The traditional wellsprings of a culture's wisdom derive from myth, with its literary descendants, and the formal science of its period. History and biography, with their claims to factuality, perhaps link the two. Add to these our individual, private experiences, often inarticulate, and we have rich potential sources for knowledge of emotional states in general, and specifically of depression. The scientific approach attempts to conceptualize and treat depression in terms of the science of the times—be it early primitive magic, or rites as part of a religious conceptual system, or what we hold today to be scientific enlightenment.

The mythic approach to depression, often linked to religion, contains a core of psychological understanding. At times, there was a search for causality in terms of human or godly responsibility—often with an admixture of punitiveness and judgmentalism. Release was sought by some expression of woe, and solace by affirmative experience. The psychoanalytic orientation at times happily unites with these varied approaches as culture-medium for its own approach, but it has no monopoly on knowledge or wisdom—or error.

WHEN ANALYSTS USED TO WRITE about writers, they were often buoyed by a conviction that they were talking about another species. Those who recall the heyday of Edmund Bergler (1949) in midcentury may also recall his extensive analysis of writers.

507

The writer acts both roles—that of the giving mother and the recipient child—on his own person. He gives to himself, out of himself, beautiful words and ideas, thus establishing an autarchy. . . . Whereas the typical neurotic needs two people (himself and an object) for unconscious reenactment of an infantile fantasy, the writer combines both roles into one. (pp. 81-82)

The insight is shrewd, but the innocence Bergler displays in not applying it to himself, an analyst said to have produced four books a year and more than three hundred papers, would be difficult to preserve today.

The old idea of the analyst as objective observer of psychic phenomena has been dethroned; we postmoderns have guillotined the neutral medium. To be consistent, we must scrutinize how ideas in psychological discourse are affected by the medium in which they appear, including writing. (Was not one of Spence’s accusations against Freud that he was too good a writer?) More typical now, a half-century after Bergler, would be this comment by Stanley Olinick (1997) in a discussion of writer’s block: “During many years, I was at times peripherally aware of writing for a vaguely defined, taciturn, critical colleague in some distant city” (p. 184). Here the analyst-writer puts himself on the line, albeit a bit gingerly. Writing is an essential means of shaping the discussion of psychoanalysis, but it is not a neutral medium. Writing in Psychoanalysis, the first volume of a monograph series called Psychoanalytic Issues published by the Italian Psychoanalytic Society, recognizes this implicitly. Its contributors try to come to terms with the fact that we have lost our innocence.

But what is writing? Antonio Alberto Semi’s chapter, “Writing in Psychoanalysis,” has a fine quotation on the subject in a letter from Freud to Fliess.

READING THIS LIVELY and unselfconscious interview made me wish I were the proverbial fly on the wall while it was taking place, eavesdropping, as it were, on a private yet meant-to-become-public, serious exchange with a touch of repartee. Not only did Dr. Issacharoff’s experience remind me of a similar one I had with Dr. Szalita some twenty years ago, but, as with many an analytic session, the flow of the question and answer continuity, the wonderment at what was pursued in preference to something else, the choice of sequence or change, made me ponder the exercise of our preferences, conscious or unconscious, in the process of our inquiry and the achievement of its purpose. It is, then, with a sense of privilege and a feeling of humility that I shall attempt what I hope to be a resonant response to the multifaceted ways in which the topic of the conversations between the two participants was addressed. In so doing, I am mindful of one of Dr. Szalita’s basic tenets, a painfully and painstakingly reached one, that “every communication has an intention, content, form, and effect.” I am also mindful of what a colleague of yore, Francis Braceland, once said: “You see, old men have trouble getting folks to listen to them, but readers are captive,” at least as they go on reading. Also, as Dr. Issacharoff warned, there is “a need to take responsibility for what you say, when you say it, in what context, and to whom.”

I MET SULLIVAN AFTER I MET Clara Thompson and Erich Fromm. My connection with analysis began when I was on the internists’ staff at Mount Sinai and got more and more fascinated with the patients in internal medicine, always looking for whatever emotional disorders were accompanying their symptoms. So with that perspective, I spoke with Dr. Myer Maskin, an analyst and psychiatrist also connected with Mount Sinai, who told me of a group, with Karen Horney, Clara Thompson, and Erich Fromm, and that he had been in analysis with Clara Thompson. I didn’t even hear the name “Sullivan” for a couple of years.

As many of us did, and many of you will do, there was an attempt to evaluate the person, the analyst you’re going to work with, in whatever way you can. There was one occasion when both Karen Horney and Clara Thompson were presenting, as might be done here, and the way their dialogue went it was as though Karen Horney was the older sister snubbing her would-be competitive younger sister, and I could see that Clara was sort of settling into herself, so I decided that Clara would be my analyst.

THE “HOW” MAKES ALL THE DIFFERENCE*

I THOUGHT I KNEW ROSE SPIEGEL. I thought I knew her well, and indeed, I spent a lot of time with her as student, supervisee, coresearcher, cowriter, and friend. I read almost everything she ever wrote that was available to me, not only in psychoanalysis and psychiatry, but in medicine and surgery, areas to which she made several significant contributions. But, for this article, an essay dedicated to her memory, I revisited some of her analytic writings on communication, and I was dazzled like a raw sophomore opening his mind to the craft of Keats. His “On First Looking Into Chapman’s Homer” is a stunning piece that has seduced many a youth into deluded fantasies of a writing career. After all, who could resist the pull of a lustrous line like, “Then felt I like some watcher of the skies / When a new planet swims into his ken”?

I thought I knew Rose, her inordinate capacity to wonder, to be curious, her consummate eagerness to play with ideas and to offer them to others, but I was startled, refreshingly surprised, to find her thoughts still incisively astute and as stimulating as ever.

THIS HUGE, EXPENSIVE, AND AMBITIOUS book contains thirty-eight chapters from thirty-seven contributors, and over nine-hundred pages of text. The large double-column format allows for more than seven-hundred words per page, so in effect, it is even larger than the number of pages indicates. The editors’ fundamental goal was to provide a “reference text” for members of the mental-health field who want to deepen their understanding of interpersonal theory and practice.

Biographies of the founders of interpersonal psychoanalysis—Sullivan, Thompson, Fromm, Fromm-Reichman, Horney, and Ferenczi—are followed by a section on metapsychological positions regarding the self, cognition, anxiety, and gender; then come four chapters on development, ten on psychopathology, six more on the analytic process, and finally five chapters on special topics, including treatment of children, adolescents, cross-cultural issues, and supervision. This is a megabook, indicative of the maturity and power of the interpersonal model in the psychoanalytic world, and specifically of the influence of the William Alanson White Institute. (Only four of the thirty-seven contributors are not directly affiliated with White.)

This review focuses on the Handbook’s psychopathology section. Comprised of ten chapters, each on a separate diagnostic group, with eleven authors and 239 pages of text, it is a complete book of human psychopathology within the Handbook.

THE PUBLICATION OF The Bonds of Love (1988) established Jessica Benjamin as a leading developer of relational psychoanalysis. The current volume is a collection of essays, most of them previously published, in which she extends her ideas regarding the tension between psychoanalysis and feminist theory. She is interested specifically in a discussion of Lacanian and object relations theories, and in delineating dilemmas of gender that can be “understood by reference to the issues of envy and loss, identification and repudiation, that object relations theory has foregrounded” (p. 15).

Benjamin intends to develop the idea of the analytic situation as intersubjective. The term, introduced in psychoanalysis by Atwood and Stolorow (1984), refers to the intersection between two subjects, as opposed to a meeting of a subject and an object. THIS BOOK, DESPITE ITS TITLE, is not for child specialists only. Although one of the major thrusts of the book is the explication of a treatment approach for infants and their parents, The Motherhood Constellation is a significant addition as well to the evolving developmental theory of parent-infant interaction. Stern once again contributes convincingly to the theoretical perspective that emphasizes early interaction as a basic building block of personality. This interactional theory, in turn, supports the many contemporary revisions of psychoanalytic technique which emphasize the relationship between patient and analyst. In this regard, Stern’s book is of value to analysts of all orientations, whether they treat children or not.

The publication of Stern’s (1985) book, The Interpersonal World of the Infant, helped to fuel the contemporary theoretical turn away from the libidinal infant and toward the interactive parent-infant dyad. Through direct extrapolations of his (and others’) work with parents and infants to the patient-analyst dyad, Stern presented compelling and comprehensive theoretical support for technical innovations that focus on the interactive psychotherapeutic dyad rather than solely on the intrapsychic patient. Just as Klein’s and Sullivan’s revisions of developmental theory led to changes in psychoanalytic technique, so Stern’s research lent additional and necessary support toward viewing the patient-analyst interaction as central—both clinically informative and therapeutically mutative.

I HAVE SAT IN MY CONSULTING ROOM and experienced the awful feeling of knowing that I have failed my patient in some important way. It has a palpable feel to it: a sinking feeling of having been the one to disappoint, to let down, to betray the trust of another. And yet, I haven’t found the term “betrayal” nor any reasonable facsimile depicted in the literature; when mentioned at all, betrayal is usually depicted as residing somehow within the patient, or within the patient’s experience. From this protective distance, we can hazard our conjectures, postulate reenactments, feel compassion for the betrayed. When I went searching for writings on betrayals within the therapeutic relationship—between patient and analyst—at first I could find nothing. I was perplexed, dismayed, and finally annoyed at our arrogance in not seeing what, to me, is an issue inherent in the process. But then I began to wonder; perhaps I was using the wrong term. I went up to the stacks and pulled down recent volumes of analytic journals, searching for some title approaching this issue. Finally I found it, and realized that I had been taking the wrong tack entirely. Apparently, what had seemed to me to be the patient’s subjective feeling of betrayal was to be explored, instead, from the analyst’s perspective, in terms of “error.” It wasn’t betrayal that I would find explored here, but “mistakes, errors, and oversights” (Levenson, 1992). And so, this omission was to become the foundation for my musings over what, for me, has the discomforting feel of betrayal.

A Bug-Free Universe

Michael Eigen Ph.D.

Michael Eigen

1225 Central Park West, Apt. 10A
New York, NY 10024

Michael Eigen  

WHY ARE THERE BUGS IN THE UNIVERSE? This is an egocentric question. Human beings are latecomers in this world, compared with bugs. But to our eyes, and especially skin, bugs are a nuisance, at times a menace. They disturb us with buzz, bite, itch, swellings, disease. We learn, too, that our world and bodies are populated by invisible as well as visible bugs, and we are unwilling hosts at their mercy.

Many years ago, as a counselor at the Henry Street Settlement House camp, I was forced to do unpleasant things, like put worms on hooks, so that disadvantaged children could have a nice time. One day in the woods we were having an especially nice time. We had gone fishing and were putting up tents for the night. Soon we would be roasting marshmallows over a fire. One of the boys, a Jehovah's Witness, broke my absorption by blurting out, “It's great. But I hate the bugs. Why do there have to be bugs?” It was an in-your-face question and I had to answer it. The boy was serious. The rest of the night hung in the balance. I shrugged, then found myself saying, “To make sure you know you’re not in heaven yet.” He nodded, and we went on with our sleepout.

In recent years, more and more patients have come in wishing for a bug-free universe. In one form or another, it is an ancient wish. Religions promise a bug-free state someday, only not now. At times, it seems, religions treat the universe as a bug to be free of—life is the bug. Some promise freedom from suffering (a bug) by following their path. My patients do not want the bug-free life later. They want it now. They do not want freedom from suffering through a discipline. They expect it just by being. They wish to wish suffering away. Deep down they feel they can will bugs out of the universe. They live by an unconscious imperative that there ought not be pain in their lives.

This contrasts with patients who are willing to suffer for the promise of getting better. There are tormented souls who laugh at painlessness. For them, agony is a necessary part of existence, of any life process. In their dreams, bugs refer to madness, and life is stamped by madness.

IN “SOME CHARACTER TYPES Met with in Psycho-Analytic Work,” Freud (1916) depicted three “surprising traits of character,” which he dubbed “The Exceptions,” “Those Wrecked by Success,” and “Criminals from a Sense of Guilt.” Freud found each of these characters in its own way a product of guilt, punishment, and reparation. Those wrecked by success—Lady Macbeth serves as an example—have prospered at the expense of others. They are therefore guilty and must suffer, hence their seemingly self-imposed denouements. The criminal has done wrong in order to make sense of “an oppressive feeling of guilt of which he did not know the origin” (p. 332). Those who except themselves from the general rules of order are exceptions in this triptych as well, in that they have not done wrong but, rather, as children were unjustly punished and now feel entitled to special privilege. Freud did not tell us for what crimes these future egoists had been chastened, but for the criminals and the wrecks he made it clear, as he so often did, that “[t]he invariable outcome of analytic work was to show that this obscure sense of guilt derived from the Oedipus complex and was a reaction to the two great criminal intentions of killing the father and having sexual relations with the mother” (pp. 332-333).

The outcome of analytic work in the latter half of our century has proved less invariable. Oedipal conflict no longer accounts for every measure of neurotic suffering, a considerable proportion of which now appears to derive from earlier epochs of development, when rivalry counts less in the psychic economy of the infant or child than does its dependency upon others. Building on current psychoanalytic viewpoints, we focus on what we consider to be the most fundamental damage done to the psychic integrity of the abuse survivor, examine some of its sources in the abuse experience, and suggest a perspective for addressing the complex clinical problems that often arise in working with survivors of sexual abuse.

Renown of that magnitude is dependent on the happy coincidence of a multitude of factors, including the right message at the most opportune time. This was no doubt true for Laing, when the student unrest of the Vietnam War intersected with his impassioned critique of a society intent on subverting the minds of its youth for unforeseen purposes. At a time when authority figures of every persuasion were suspect, the so-called counterculture embraced this disarming Scotsman and trusted him to explain how they were being mystified and why. IN THE FIRST PARAGRAPH OF HIS ARTICLE, Hirsch refers to me as having accomplished a radical reworking of the role of the analyst in the clinical dyad. When I read this description of myself, I was flooded with a warm feeling of goodwill toward Hirsch and anything he intended to say. In that mood, I read the rest of his article and formulated my response to it. In other words, the remarks that follow should be understood to come from a definite Irwin Hirsch well-wisher. I mention this observation concerning my participation as reader, in a dyad with Hirsch as author, in the spirit of his subject: Hirsch’s emphasis, after all, is on the analyst as an observing participant in dyadic relationships.

In the same vein, I can report that my sympathy toward Hirsch persisted undiminished, even when I realized that he was congratulating me on having reinvented the wheel—on having recognized for myself what analysts of the interpersonalist school had been talking about for decades. Why was I not put out to discover that Hirsch is essentially damning me with faint praise? To begin with, because I think he’s right. Obviously, parochialism is the bane of psychoanalytic discourse. During my years in training at the San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute, I don’t think I was assigned a single article from Contemporary Psychoanalysis to read. How was I to know about Wolstein or Levenson? Had I become acquainted with their work earlier, it surely would have speeded up the development of my own thinking.

Another reason why being revealed as a Johnny-come-lately doesn’t bother me is that I’m not nearly as concerned in general as Hirsch is about priorities and citation. SUPERVISION AND SEXUAL ABUSE*

A SIXTIES ROCK BAND ONCE ASKED something like, “How do you do what you do when you do what you do to me? I wish I knew.” This convoluted lyric could serve well as the underpinning of this article, which examines the supervisory relationship when the supervisee is an analyst working with an adult survivor of childhood sexual abuse. To do justice to this topic, positioned as it is at the rather congested intersection of psychoanalytic views of both supervision and the treatment of early sexual trauma, it is helpful first to address each subject independently. I begin, therefore, by discussing supervision from a relational perspective; I then offer my thinking on the particular complexities added to the relational fields of supervisor-analyst-patient when the analyst is treating an adult survivor of childhood sexual abuse. Supervisory and clinical material are used to illustrate the theoretical points made.

The analytic process, in this view, encompasses a dialectical volleying between enactment and observation, or interpretation, of that which has been put in play between the members of the analytic dyad. DR. HIRSCH HAS WRITTEN an extremely interesting, thought-provoking article that traces the development of the concept of enactment within the “traditional” or “classical” form of psychoanalysis, relating it to the thinking of the post-Sullivan interpersonal school. He demonstrates how the two theoretical points of view converge in their understanding of interpersonal and interpsychic phenomenon, making the point that if traditionally trained analysts had been more open to interpersonal psychoanalysis, they would have appreciated the analyst’s inevitable subjectivity, the patient’s sensitivity to the affect and desires of the analyst, and the analyst’s contribution to analytic material, much sooner. In his focus on the demonization of the interpersonal school by the traditional one, he emphasizes the benefits a greater familiarity with the literature of interpersonal psychoanalysis would have provided. With this I cannot help but agree. What is true for psychoanalysis is also true for many areas of both the sciences and humanities; a wish to maintain a belief in the correctness of one’s training and theoretical assumptions frequently leads to an avoidance, if not an absolute condemnation, of all that challenges it.

Fortunately, we seem to be entering a new era of psychoanalytic thought. For most of us, psychoanalysis no longer is a panacea for every form of psychopathology. We no longer try to fit patients to the treatment.

WORK WITH A PATIENT WITH SCHIZOPHRENIA AND OBSESSIVE COMPULSIVE DISORDER

IN THE THREE SECTIONS of this article I summarize the history and evolution of Chestnut Lodge (Silver, 1989), present aspects of my ten-year ongoing treatment of a woman with both schizophrenia and obsessive compulsive disorder, and then comment on the work. The Lodge opened in 1910. It has had four medical directors: Ernest Bullard, then his son Dexter, Sr., then the latter’s oldest son Dexter, Jr., and now Wayne Fenton. Each is a forceful and creative representative of his times. It has had five directors of psychotherapy: Frieda Fromm-Reichmann, then Otto Will, Ping-Nie Pao, Robert Cohen, and now E. James Anthony in the adolescent hospital and Christopher Keats in the adult hospital. Tracing the orientations and written contributions of each of these clinicians provides a history of the Lodge (Fromm-Reichmann 1950; D. Bullard, 1959; Sacksteder, Schwartz & Akanabe, 1987; Pao, 1979; McGlashan & Keats, 1989; Anthony, 1990). It is a microcosm and model of American psychiatry, with a proud record of primary influence in two branches, one administrative, the other academic or theoretical. Currently, as throughout the mental-health field in the United States, we struggle to accommodate to rapidly shifting, externally imposed changes. Life is more hectic, less centered. Lodge clinicians usually work elsewhere part of the time, and have less time to confer with each other. We are burdened with nostalgia and grief. Our mentors have all died or retired. The Lodge boundaries probably will soon shrink from sixty to twenty acres. Our nonhuman environment (Searles, 1960) is diminishing.

The founder, Ernest Bullard, had previously been Superintendent of the Wisconsin State Hospital for the Insane, across Lake Mendota from Madison. He believed both in rest cure and work therapy, saying that it is better for people to grow real roses than to make artificial ones (E. Bullard, 1916), neatly foreshadowing Joanne Greenberg’s (1964) autobiographic novel from the Lodge, I Never Promised You a Rose Garden.

Lawrence Josephs

Lawrence Josephs, Ph.D.
Derner Institute of Advanced Psychological Studies
Adelphi University
Garden City, NY 11530

Lawrence Josephs  

THE CONSCIOUS BELIEFS and convictions that people entertain in regard to their own psychological functioning may be significantly influenced by their relationship to others, by how others view their own psychological functioning. Psychoanalysts have long been concerned about the nature of the analytic relationship, in which the patient’s conscious beliefs and convictions about the nature of her own unconscious processes evolve. Since the beginning of psychoanalysis, there has been a concern that when the patient’s conscious beliefs about her own psychological functioning have evolved in the context of an unanalyzed transference of authority, these beliefs may reflect a sort of false consciousness, based upon unconscious compliance to the analyst’s presumed wishes and expectations. As psychoanalysis evolved from the pressure techniques of hypnosis into the method of free association, with the analysis of resistance and transference, it was hoped that a method was evolving that would analyze, rather than exploit, the patient’s transference of authority to the analyst. The transference of authority was to be dissolved through its analysis; thus the results of psychoanalysis could not be attributed to the patient’s suggestibility to the analyst’s interpretations.

With the evolution from a one-person to a two-person psychology, it became apparent that a one-person psychology tends to de-emphasize the influence of the analyst’s participation in the analytic situation. It was assumed that an essentially neutral and abstinent analyst will minimally influence the natural unfolding of the patient’s free associations, transferences, and resistances. A two-person psychology will recognize that the analyst’s personality, countertransference, theoretical beliefs, nonverbal communication, and verbal interpretations will all crucially shape the free associations, resistances, and transferences that emerge in the course of the treatment.

Now, in a line of associations ambiguous words (or, as we may call them, “switch-words”) act like points at a junction. Psychoanalysis Makes a Map

Toward the end of his hilarious Small World, which spoofs the international academic conference circuit, David Lodge (1984) constructs an antic scene that could not have been written had not both psychoanalysis and feminism pervaded academia in particular, and intellectual life in general. Angelica, a rising literary critic, is presenting a paper on the genre of romance (the novel in which she appears is, after all, subtitled An Academic Romance) at the Modern Language Association. Rife with sexual reference, her essay reveals the woman who, at once central and marginal to psychoanalytic thought, has uneasily entered the psychoanalytic stage, glad to have joined the nervously welcoming company of players, but not wholly sure that it's a good idea.

Angelica's theory unfolds in terms whose debt to Sigmund Freud states itself.

If epic is a phallic genre, which can hardly be denied, and tragedy the genre of castration (we are none of us, I suppose, deceived by the selfblinding of Oedipus as to the true nature of the wound he is impelled to inflict upon himself, or likely to overlook the symbolic equivalence between eyeballs and testicles) then surely there is no doubt that romance is a supremely invaginated mode of narrative. BY NOW IT HAS BECOME A COMMONPLACE of epistemological debate to assail the traditional scientific paradigm by acknowledging the role of the observer in determining the nature of the observed. Whether the expert theories of the scientist or the folk theories of ordinary people, such theories, so the story goes, are based on a set of fundamental assumptions that provide interpretive principles in terms of which particular events are necessarily understood. From this perspective, there are no facts that are independent of the knower-scientist-investigator. All aspects of knowledge or understanding require acts of interpretation that depend on the investigator’s precritical assumptions.

The consequence of this antiempiricist or constructivist theory of science for psychoanalytic psychology has involved a profound restructuring of disciplinary self-understanding, moving away from an enterprise whose primary task was conceived as the reconstruction of a single, definitive life history, based on the uncovering of brute facts by a neutral or evenly hovering therapist. Steven Frankel  

DISRUPTIONS IN PSYCHOANALYTIC WORK go by many names, depending on the theory and the alleged source of the problem. Transferences originate within the analysand and may shatter cooperative engagement with the analyst. Problematic countertransferences are contributed by the analyst, as a reflection of projective identification orchestrated by the patient or of the analyst’s transferences. Unsettling enacted unconscious scenarios originate primarily in the analyst, analysand, or both. An intersubjective perspective has each partner influencing and deflecting the other. Their individual contributions are inseparable. A point of view that emphasizes discontinuity in experience substitutes dissociation for repression. The analyst represents a way of being that is foreign to the patient’s sense of self. The analyst may be invested with dissociated aspects of the analysand’s self. In either case, the analysand assiduously resists joining with the analyst.

The point is that disruptions are complex events with hard-to-separate contributions by analyst and analysand. My impression is that most disruptions in psychoanalysis are resolved spontaneously with little or no analytic exploration. Often this process is unnoticed and unacknowledged. It occurs through subtle interactions, and it hardly matters how analytical and dispassionate the analyst attempts to be.

In this article I argue that the facilitating activity that characterizes these subtle realignments should be part of analytic technique. Being helpful and concerned is not antianalytic. When the analyst accepts this role (at times, the analysand takes the initiative), the analysand is likely to feel safer, better understood, and cared about. The result, barring paradoxical neurotic developments, will be to reinforce the analysand’s confidence that the analysis is on track. Rather than being discouraged from reengaging in analytic exploration, the analysand is more likely to undertake it.

WHEN FREUD VIEWED DREAMS as “the royal road to the unconscious,” he inestimably prized dreams as the primary avenue to the unconscious. He envisioned the unconscious to be a wellspring of instinctual energies pressing for discharge and a container of fantasies and memories banned from consciousness. The dynamic unconscious provided an explanation for the pervasive irrationality in human beings and was considered by Freud to be one of the three great scientific discoveries (the others by Copernicus and Darwin) that dethroned human beings from their exalted status.

It has been close to a century since Freud published his monumental work on dreams, a work about which Freud stated, “Insight such as this falls to one’s lot but once in a lifetime” (Jones, 1953, p. 350). Remarkably, the classical model of dream formation and interpretation has remained relatively unchanged (Curtis & Sachs, 1976). Detachment And Continuity

Robert Gaines Ph.D

Robert Gaines

Robert Gaines, Ph.D
27 West 72nd Street
New York, NY 10023

Robert Gaines  

Summary

The idea that the major task of mourning is detachment from the lost object has been examined critically. Mourning is more accurately conceived of as involving both processes of “letting go” and of “holding on.” Loss of an object threatens inner object ties and identifications, which are the basis of a secure inner world and a sense of security in the world. Mastery of this threat is achieved through the process I have termed the creation of continuity. Creation of continuity is distinguished from the various forms of denial of loss by the fact that in creating continuity there is always explicit, even if unconscious, recognition that the object is gone. Creation of continuity always has a bittersweet quality, but, in tandem with the process of detachment, it helps the mourner move forward in life.

The process of creating continuity is often carried out smoothly and without conscious awareness, but it does require psychological work. At other times a person may suffer feelings or symptoms that reflect a failure to maintain continuity, and this can seriously complicate mourning. Awareness of the task of creating continuity and its possible derailment can be helpful in treating complicated mourning. For instance, an overemphasis on conflicts around the need to detach can exacerbate mourning complications that derive from difficulty maintaining continuity. The perspective on mourning that develops from consideration of the task of creating continuity also heightens awareness that mourning is not something accomplished in one period of time and then left behind. While the acute phase of grief comes to an end, the challenge of coping with a loss continues throughout the lifespan.

A FIFTEEN-YEAR PERSPECTIVE*

AIDS HAS CHANGED ALL OF US, as mental-health professionals, as individual human beings, and as a society. Twenty years ago, none of us thought we would see so many hundreds of thousands of relatively young people dying of a communicable disease. AIDS has really humbled us. Through most of modern Western history there have been serious venereal diseases that were incurable. Many of us who came of age in the postpenicillin generation enjoyed a very brief, unusual window in the history of time, a time when it seemed that there were no fatal venereal diseases, and in which we thought there would be no more. We became arrogant in our faith in modern medicine. AIDS shocked us from our arrogance. It returned the specter of incurable venereal disease to us, and reminded us that nature is a formidable and clever adversary to human medicine, and will probably always stay one step ahead of man. Besides the terrible losses that we all have had to face, AIDS has forced psychological changes in all of us. It has forced us to rethink our relation to sickness and health, to mortality, sexuality, drug use, and what we consider valuable in life.

In this article I will address many aspects of AIDS, beginning with some historical perspective. I will tell, from my own viewpoint, how the AIDS epidemic evolved and how psychological attitudes, among patients and all of society, have shifted. DISCUSSION OF ANN SILVER

I AM DELIGHTED TO BE DISCUSSING Dr. Silver’s article. I first met Dr. Silver about ten years ago in Washington, and I was immediately taken with her clinical thinking and her wonderful lack of pretense. We sent each other reprints, and I was startled that although we had never had a clinical discussion, we had come up with similar ideas about working with psychotic and borderline patients. I realized how connected we were, through our heritage in the interpersonal tradition—hers in the Washington area and mine in New York. Both of us had teachers who studied and worked with Frieda Fromm-Reichmann and Harry Stack Sullivan.

A review of Attachment Theory: Social, Developmental, and Clinical Perspectives, edited by Susan Goldberg, Roy Muir, and John Kerr. Hillsdale, NJ: The Analytic Press, 1995. 528 pp.

Sandra Buechler Ph.D.

Sandra Buechler

Sandra Buechler, Ph.D.

Sandra Buechler  

AS ANALYSTS, myopia is one condition we must avoid. We are called upon to deal with a vast array of entrenched difficulties and must be open to any information that could be of use in our work. We can afford neither the narrow departmentalism of academia nor the rigid religiosity that some analytic circles still require of adherents.

157

For this reason, the story of John Bowlby’s relationship to the analytic world is a sad, shameful chapter in our history. As recounted in this recent volume, Bowlby’s is the story of a man ostracized from the British Psychoanalytic Society once his unpopular views on attachment became known. In a sympathetic chapter (pp. 19-43) written with literary finesse, Jeremy Holmes tells how Bowlby’s interests in psychoanalysis and processes of attachment grew. Holmes freely speculates about possible roots of Bowlby’s interests in his childhood, recounts his growing up and his analytic training (with Joan Riviere as his analyst) in a British Psychoanalytic Society torn between adherents of Melanie Klein and Anna Freud. At first, Bowlby was able to navigate well in this atmosphere, but his interpersonal rather than intrapsychic, and reality- rather than fantasy-based theories were soon met with skepticism and then with a kind of silent wall of ostracism by the largely Kleinian analytic community. Only in 1980 did he begin to receive recognition at home for his ground breaking research. It would be useful if we could learn from those twenty years in which both psychoanalysis and attachment theory suffered because of an insecure analytic climate in which provocative ideas could not be considered.

Bowlby’s story forms the backdrop for the contributions in this richly rewarding volume. Actually the book developed out of a conference held in 1993 in Toronto, which had as its express purpose the interaction of clinicians and researchers in the common pursuit of an understanding of the processes of attachment.

The contributors study attachment from ethological, psychoanalytic, and developmental perspectives. The first several chapters review the history of attachment theory from its origins in Bowlby’s ethologically based understanding of the primary mother-child bond. While Bowlby focused on the survival functions of that bond and the effects on the child of major disruptions, his colleague Mary Ainsworth devised an experimental paradigm (the “Strange Situation”) to explore differences in how infants respond to short separations from their primary caregivers. Ainsworth’s paradigm has provided a way to classify a particular infant’s separation behavior, enabling subsequent researchers to investigate what can be predicted about the child’s later development from his pattern of separation responses at an early age. Another fundamental tool, the Adult Attachment Interview, created by Mary Main, allowed investigators to study the interaction between infant and parent attachment styles.

REPLY TO CHUSED AND RENIK

I THANK THE EDITORIAL BOARD of Contemporary Psychoanalysis for inviting me to write my original article, for asking two such esteemed analysts to comment, and for welcoming my reply. I also thank Judith Chused and Owen Renik for their careful reading, their provocative and thoughtful challenges, and their courteous and respectful attitudes. Both have provoked me to refine my thinking. I here compare the positions of Chused and Renik with each other and respond to their comments about my article.

Chused and Renik have very different ways of defining and speaking about enactments, and this also bears on their comments to me. Chused defines enactments as actualizations of the transference. This phenomenon occurs periodically and reflects a lapse in the analyst’s control over countertransference. This analytic problem can be converted into a gain if the analyst eventually detects it and interprets it as a jointly constructed acting-in of key themes in the patient’s internal world. This is similar to Edgar Levenson’s concept of transformation and Joseph Sandler’s role responsiveness. Neither of these theorists, however, place the negative cast of lapse on this interaction, for they see such enmeshments as not only inevitable but at the core of mutative action. Both also view enactments as in process much of the time, more of an everyday phenomenon than Chused’s description of unusual moments. As I understand Renik, enactment is synonomous with the concepts of subjectivity and of countertransference. Renik’s irreducible subjectivity depicts an analyst who is always countertransfering. Dale Ortmeyer  

THE EARLY INTERPERSONALISTS*

LOOKING BACK AT THE FORTY-THREE YEARS since Clara Thompson became the first president of The William Alanson White Psychoanalytic Society in 1952, and wanting a view of our future in the twenty-first century, we think of revisiting history. The seriousness and dedication of such a task is, without question, valid. As new data becomes available from previously unpublished records and there is continued remembrance of things past, this begs for deconstruction of old meanings and the structuring of new hypotheses that more completely and consistently fit the information at hand. It is a rational approach to rewriting history. It is valid. Kotre's (1995) work on memory supports this approach. He writes that the “remembering self” has the aforementioned function of a keeper of the archives, fastidiously guarding original records. Whereas Kotre is using this function as an autobiographical search for personal past experience, I am extrapolating its use to the biographical search for experience of the lives of the early interpersonalists. Kotre goes on to say that another function of the remembering self is to seek a comprehensive view of reality, generating a story, a myth that turns events into symbols and metaphors. It is the myth I now pursue, returning to the archives later. As George Vaillant (1977) poetically says, once a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, it remembers being a little butterfly.

It is this story-telling approach to the past in the present, an intuitive approach, that is captured in the words of T.S. Eliot (1952) in his Four Quartets when he says

We shall not cease from exploration
And the end of all our exploring
Will be to arrive where we started

Charles Spezzano  

ARNOLD ROTHSTEIN HAS WRITTEN a unique, provocative, and clinically useful book. His topic is the creation of an analytic process with new patients who want their treatment to be conducted in some way other than what the analyst recommends. For Rothstein, this usually means that they want lower fees, less frequent sessions, or a chair instead of the couch. Readers, however, will find that his thinking about and handling of those particular disagreements are applicable to virtually any disparity between how clinician and patient want to proceed.

Rothstein aims to enhance our ability to open an analytic process in which there is an opportunity to understand patients’ motives for not wanting to follow the recommendation of the professional they consult and whose opinion about treatment they have requested. The catalysts for writing the book appear to be (1) several studies over the last two decades which indicate that most analysts spend much time doing clinical work that they do not consider to be psychoanalysis; (2) Rothstein’s success in keeping his own practice filled with analytic cases (ten, in fact); and (3) his belief that when prospective patients say they want once- or twice-weekly treatment, to sit up, and a reduced fee, too often we meet such confusion and ambivalence with our own; we fail to hold in our minds with conviction, and to convey to prospective analysands with confidence, the attitude that analysis is likely to be the optimal treatment for what ails them and that a trial of it should be undertaken.
